title: Breaking and Entering: Acopia on Friendship, Transience, and the Things Left Unsaid
transcript:
Kate Durman and Morgan Wright of Acopia joined Lauren Taylor in the Triple R studios ahead of the band's sold-out show at the Night Cat. Broadcast on Breaking and Entering, Triple R, 18 June 2026.

Lauren: I'm joined in the RRR studios at the moment by a couple of members of the local trio Acopia. I've got Kate Durman and Morgan Wright with me in the studio. Thanks for joining me, guys.

Guest: It's a pleasure to be here. Thanks for having us.

Lauren: We should mention the other member of your trio, Lachlan, unfortunately unwell and unable to join us today. But thanks very much for dropping by Breaking and Entering. I know your show has sold out at the Night Cat, so you're not here with anything to promote, just having a chat. And of course, you've been up to quite a bit recently. Some big tours with Acopia, making really great waves overseas now as well. You got back from a couple of months away on a North American tour, UK and Europe as well. Is it nice to be back in your hometown for a bit now?

Guest: It is. I personally really miss the food a lot. Most of all — oh, most of all my friends, probably. But the produce and food was a close second. Not to be ungrateful. It was an amazing tour, and it was a really positive experience. So grateful to have gone there.

Lauren: Do you have first places that you go to when you tour overseas, to orient yourself in a new city? I know lots of people like to start at record stores, or something like that.

Guest: Probably just a good pub meal or something. Or Pret. Yeah, in Europe or the UK. So good.

Guest: We should do that, though. That's actually wise. That sounds way smarter. Do stuff like that.

Lauren: How do the members of Acopia go touring together? Is it all pretty smooth sailing?

Guest: It's pretty good. Now we've done a few international tours, and have spent a lot of time around each other, in each other's pockets. And I would say by now we can read each other very well. For instance, noticing when we need to give each other a bit of space.

Guest: Yeah, definitely. We all need quite a bit of space, so we get to have a lot of downtime and do our own thing. But always going and eating dinners and stuff together, which is really nice.

Lauren: Excellent. You've described working with Acopia as a surreal experience, writing music with your best friends. What is it about the experience of writing together that feels so surreal or unique?

Kate: I'll let you answer that, Morgan. That's for you.

Morgan: Thank you, Kate. I think primarily the fact that it's really fun and actually enjoyable. I think sometimes collaborating can be a bit of a slog. But I think what makes it really easy for the project is the fact that all of us can play instruments and produce. So if we want to communicate an idea, we can do words, but then you can also just show each other the idea. And that's a really, I think like…

[Unclear audio at 00:03:29–00:03:31]

Lauren: Looking back over three albums that you've done together now, does your personal history and friendship shape the sound of Acopia in a way that maybe you might not have anticipated?

Guest: Well, I guess, like I was saying, we spend a lot of time, in a positive way, by the way. We spend a lot of time together, and our friendship with each other is all very strong because of that, and might not have been as strong if we weren't doing this project together.

[Unclear audio at 00:04:02–00:04:04]

Lauren: In terms of the sound, though.

[Unclear audio at 00:04:06–00:04:09]

Morgan: I think, yeah, definitely. I feel like whenever we make music, we always spend probably a quarter of the time debriefing emotionally about stuff that's stressing us out, but also talking about just everything happening in the world. So I think as we're going to be affected by everything around us as humans, that's going to impact our craft. I think as the albums have gone along, you kind of can communicate that maybe a bit clearer, or we're all maybe better at channelling, say, a certain emotion, or trying to elicit a certain emotion in the listener through the songwriting or through the production. I feel like we're much better at that now.

Lauren: All three members are really accomplished electronic producers in your own right too. You've had individual projects that are going on outside of Acopia. Kate with Purient, who we heard from a bit earlier in the show today. Lachlan, who isn't here, but one half of Tambo's House with River Yarra. And Morgan, you're releasing music under your own name as well. And you've said that Acopia was born from a shared curiosity in the genre's softer, ethereal corners, outside of the club space. Can you talk about what drew you to that side of the music, and how that shared interest evolved into the creative vision behind the band?

Guest: Yeah, I think initially we all just really wanted to collaborate together. And because of our own projects being in the dance music world, we were kind of set on, or fixated even on, having slower songs, like 80, 90, 100 BPM. And I think that naturally had us gravitating to the more, potentially, especially for the first record, having elements of trip-hop more so, and slowed-down breakbeats, because we'd all been producing faster music with breakbeats. And then we all have a strong affection for some of the same bands, in particular Radio Dept.

So I think as the records are being written and evolved, we're starting to learn more about one another's music tastes in the softer side of music, rather than just sharing club tracks or whatever. And then COVID kind of happened maybe a year after the band had started. And I think that as well changed the songs that we wrote, leaning into that more home listening, chilled-out sound.

Lauren: You were talking before about emotions. Are there specific emotions or environments you're trying to evoke through Acopia when you're stepping away from that traditional late-night energy?

[Unclear audio at 00:07:21–00:07:23]

Kate: I guess it's just going inwards a bit more, just as a whole, as a concept even. And like you were saying, Morgan, about how we kind of debrief a lot of the time before we go into writing something, I think it's helped us become more open people. And so maybe, yeah, maybe that. Did that make sense?

[Unclear audio at 00:07:46–00:07:48]

Guest: I hope so. I've forgotten the question now. What was the question?

Guest: Me too.

Lauren: No, you answered it very well. Some people have identified your music as having this really dreamlike quality to it as well. And you mentioned going inward: are dreams an important source of information or inspiration for Acopia at all?

Guest: I feel like maybe thematically sometimes, fragmented bits of dreams or ideas or feelings. But I mean, there's been a couple of times where I, or one of us, has had a dream about a song or an idea, and we've worked on it. Can't say it has been good, but we've done it before.

Guest: Yeah. I think my dreams relating to Acopia are all just airport-related stress dreams, like forgetting my passport or something like that.

[Unclear audio at 00:08:48–00:08:51]

Lauren: Your album title, Blush Response, which was an album of the week last year, references the phrase from Blade Runner. It's used in this test to distinguish humans from replicants, measuring their emotional reactions. What drew you specifically to that concept, and how does the title connect to maybe themes or emotions you're exploring on this record?

Morgan: I'll let you handle that one, Kate. You came up with the idea.

Kate: I was re-watching the original Blade Runner, and it's one of the phrases that they use quite early on. And I just thought it was a cool concept, because it's trying to work out if something is — what was the word? Not robot, a replicant, whatever that means. I just thought about it as an emotional thing, like maybe some people that have difficulty with connecting to certain emotions, and needing to kind of sit with it for a bit to work out what they're really feeling or experiencing. And it's something that I've experienced before. I just thought it kind of sounded like what the album sounds like, in a way.

Lauren: You've also mentioned the idea of blushing itself being a really raw and involuntary thing, and a true reminder that you're alive. That's a really interesting idea, of blushing being that exact moment that an internal feeling becomes this external reaction. What was it about that idea that resonated so strongly?

Guest: It's just really cute. Blushing is really cute, and having a crush on someone's really cute, and it makes you feel alive. And a lot of our songs are love songs, or kind of about breakup, or learning who you are and what you're about. So I think it's just that, really.

Lauren: The track we're about to hear in a minute, 'Talk About It', you've said explores fears of emotional intimacy, and the piling weight of all things left unspoken. Can you maybe share a bit more about that track, and why was that something you felt drawn to exploring?

Guest: I think at the time I — oh, wait, maybe it was [name uncertain: “lucky”] at the time. I hope he won't mind me saying this. We were in the room starting to write this idea, and he was in a bit of a funk, and we're like, “What's going on?” And he said, “I don't want to talk about it.” And I was like, boom. [Unclear audio at 00:11:22–00:11:25] Write that down. Someone write that down.

[Unclear audio at 00:11:26–00:11:28]

Lauren: That's it. And the location for the recording sounds really interesting as well. You've described it as looking like a nineties movie set of a washed-up office building in South Yarra, and knowing that the building itself is set for demolition.

Guest: It's not there anymore. It's not there. You can't even go there.

Lauren: Did knowing that the space would soon be gone influence your mindset at all during those recording sessions?

Guest: I think so. Because it's weird to go into a space when you know it's going to not be there anymore. It's kind of like when you think about time and how short it is, not to get on that level, but yeah, it was cool. The days were numbered there, so we had to just be in it.

Guest: Get the record done. Yeah. And the aura was kind of threatening in there. If all the lights were on, fluorescent white lights, there were still computers, old computers. It was very weird, but cool energy.

Guest: Yeah. Threatening, but cool. It's gone now, but it's gone.

Lauren: So do you think that sense of transience makes its way onto the record?

Guest: Yeah, I think so. That's a good word. I like that one.

[Unclear audio at 00:12:46–00:12:50]

Lauren: Well, I want to say a very big thank you to our guests today, Morgan and Kate from Acopia, for dropping by and having a chat with me ahead of the sold-out shows at the Night Cat next Friday. The record is Blush Response. We're going to lift a track from it, the one we were just talking about, called 'Talk About It'. Thanks so much, guys.

Guest: Thank you for having us.

[Unclear audio at 00:13:11–01:16:56]
